clue.text: Fiddler occupying one roof

indicators.note: the answer sits inside, occupying, the run of letters across the words one roof

explanation.surface: A violinist has taken up residence under a single roof.
explanation.walkthrough: The emperor is said to have fiddled while Rome burned, so 'Fiddler' is a fair nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman emperor is famous in legend for playing music while his city burned, hence a fiddler.

clue.text: Sure about supporting football club during no-score draw? Yes, sure

indicators.note: in a down clue the later piece sits under, supporting, the earlier one
the club's letters come in the middle of the draw's two noughts

parts.note: a nil-nil draw is written 0-0, two O shapes

indicators.note: about here means turned around or rearranged, so the word sure is shuffled

explanation.surface: A confident remark about backing a club in a goalless draw, ending in emphatic agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' shuffles SURE into URSE, which goes under OFCO.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an emphatic way of agreeing, the same as 'yes, certainly'.

clue.text: Entertain with piano on hire

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece placed on another sits above it

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
to lease something is to hire it

explanation.surface: Someone rents a piano to keep guests amused.
explanation.definitionFit: To entertain someone is to give them pleasure, to delight them.

clue.text: Cor blimey! No Brit hums out 7's response to 19

indicators.note: out signals the remaining letters being knocked out of shape and rearranged
no Brit means the word for a Brit is taken away from the exclamation

parts.note: limey is old American slang for a British person
taken as written

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise from someone who hums when nobody British is around.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing LIMEY from CORBLIMEY leaves CORB; with HUMS, 'out' rearranges these. In the cartoon Danger Mouse, the hamster Penfold (7) says this whenever danger (19) looms.
explanation.definitionFit: Penfold's catchphrase of dismay in the cartoon is his usual reply when his boss faces peril.

clue.text: Name of modern establishment

indicators.note: of means taken from within the words that follow, which hide the answer

explanation.surface: A label for a newly founded institution.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a man's first name, as in the hero of Wilde's comedy about being earnest.

clue.text: See 14
Patiently starting to hug hamster …

indicators.note: starting means just the opening letter of the word patiently

parts.note: to enfold someone is to wrap them in a hug

explanation.surface: Someone waits patiently before cuddling a pet hamster.
explanation.walkthrough: Penfold is the hamster sidekick in the British cartoon Danger Mouse, the puzzle's theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Penfold is the timid hamster assistant to Danger Mouse in the cartoon series.

clue.text: … that's confused, short of time and a little nervous, in general

indicators.note: confused signals the remaining letters being jumbled
short of time means the abbreviation for time is dropped

parts.note: that refers back to the hamster at the end of the previous clue

indicators.note: a little of the word nervous is only its first letter

explanation.surface: The hamster is muddled, pressed for time and slightly jumpy, all in all.
explanation.walkthrough: HAMSTER less T gives HAMSER, which 'confused' turns into SHERMA; add N. The ellipsis carries the hamster over from 7 across.
explanation.definitionFit: William Tecumseh Sherman was a Union general in the American Civil War.

clue.text: Car in front of pillar box, wingless and slow too

indicators.note: the front of pillar is just its first letter
wingless means each word loses its outer letters, its wings; too says slow is treated the same way as box

explanation.surface: A car pulls up by a postbox, crawling slowly as well.
explanation.walkthrough: A pillar box is a British red street postbox. Losing its ends, box gives O and slow gives LO.
explanation.definitionFit: The Polo is a small hatchback made by Volkswagen.

clue.text: Part of ship where you might find tennis shoes and chair

definitions.meaning: the open deck towards the stern of a vessel

definitions.text: where you might find tennis shoes and chair
definitions.meaning: the words tennis, shoes and chair each follow deck: deck tennis, deck shoes, deckchair

explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as 'after deck': each of the three words comes after deck to make a familiar phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The rear deck of a vessel, abaft the bridge, is named for its position towards the stern.

clue.text: Cut short old car's MOT perhaps, as exterior in most messy state

indicators.note: as exterior means the test word wraps around the shortened car

parts.note: the MOT is the British annual roadworthiness test for vehicles

indicators.note: cut short means the car's name loses its final letter

parts.note: the Anglia was a Ford family car of the 1950s and 60s

explanation.surface: An old banger's roadworthiness test came out the worst-looking shambles.
explanation.walkthrough: The British MOT is the annual check every older car must pass.
explanation.definitionFit: Something most tangled is in the messiest, most knotted condition.

clue.text: Somewhat dotty detective?

definitions.meaning: the telegraph code is made partly of dots, along with dashes
Inspector ... is the Oxford detective of Colin Dexter's novels and the TV series

explanation.surface: A sleuth who is a little eccentric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dotty' looks like 'mad', but it means made of dots, like the code.
explanation.definitionFit: The code of dots and dashes shares its name with Colin Dexter's Oxford inspector.

clue.text: See 19
A spy chief enters agent's new forms of ID

indicators.note: the a and spy chief go into the middle of the rearranged letters
new signals the letters of agents being made into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: M is the head of the secret service in the Bond stories

explanation.surface: A senior spymaster slips into an agent's freshly forged identity papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges AGENTS into NETAGS, and AM 'enters' after the N.
explanation.definitionFit: Labels worn at events bearing your name serve as a simple identification.

clue.text: Uncle Sam's bill from Evian?

parts.note: naive, which is ..., written ... to front gives the water brand's name

explanation.surface: An American banknote from the French mineral water company.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as instructions: green (naive) back gives EVIAN. Baron Greenback is the villain in Danger Mouse.
explanation.definitionFit: A dollar bill is called this for the green ink printed on its reverse.

clue.text: Regime to regret around Leatherhead

indicators.note: around means the regret word goes round the letter

parts.note: to rue something is to regret it
read as leather's head, the first letter of leather; Leatherhead is also a Surrey town

explanation.surface: Someone regrets a regime imposed around a Surrey town.
explanation.definitionFit: Rule is government or a governing system, the same as a regime.

clue.text: Paul's companion still tans unevenly

indicators.note: unevenly means taking the odd-numbered letters, first, third, fifth and so on

explanation.surface: Someone's friend Paul's companion still has a patchy suntan.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Acts of the Apostles, Silas travels with Paul on his missionary journeys.

clue.text: Toilet's out of order, blocked by model's 17 across

indicators.note: blocked by means the model letter is stuck inside the jumbled letters
out of order signals the letters of toilets being jumbled

parts.note: the Model T was Ford's famous early car

explanation.surface: A lavatory is out of service, clogged by a fashion model's shoe.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the answer to 17 across, heel. Stiletto is also Baron Greenback's henchman in Danger Mouse.
explanation.definitionFit: A stiletto is a tall, thin type of shoe heel.

clue.text: Scumbag in wingless car?

indicators.note: wingless means the outer letters, the wings, are removed

parts.note: wheels is slang for a car

explanation.surface: A rotter sits in a car stripped of its wings.
explanation.definitionFit: A heel is a contemptible, untrustworthy person, a cad.

clue.text: Like arms of female, 100, going round supermarket

indicators.note: the female and hundred go round the shop's name

parts.note: her is the female pronoun
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
Aldi is a discount supermarket chain

explanation.surface: A woman of a hundred wanders round the supermarket.
explanation.definitionFit: Coats of arms belong to heraldry, so anything relating to arms is heraldic.

clue.text: Closing time having passed, left drink unopened

parts.note: someone who has passed away is dead

indicators.note: unopened means the drink loses its first letter

parts.note: wine is a drink

explanation.surface: At closing time, after the bar shut, someone left a drink untouched.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadline is the time by which something must be finished, the cut-off.

clue.text: Secret agent plants bug during a rounders game, then runs away

indicators.note: to plant something is to put it in place, here inside other letters
during means the bug comes in the midst of the other letters
game, as in a game leg, means lame or damaged, so the letters are rearranged
away means the runs are taken out

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs, so two runs are two Rs
a germ is a bug, as in a stomach bug

explanation.surface: A spy hides a listening device in the middle of a rounders match, then flees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'away' takes out both runs, and 'game' (lame, as in a game leg) rearranges the rest into DANOUSE; 'plants' and 'during' set the bug inside. Rounders is a British bat-and-ball game like baseball.
explanation.definitionFit: Danger Mouse is the cartoon world's greatest secret agent, the eyepatched hero of the series.

clue.text: Lawyers working for bigwig

parts.note: the Bar is the body of barristers
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: Lawyers are working for an important client.
explanation.walkthrough: Baron Greenback is the villain of Danger Mouse.
explanation.definitionFit: A baron is a powerful magnate, as in a press baron, so an important person.

clue.text: Smile about broken deadline in madhouse

indicators.note: about means the smile word goes round the other letters

parts.note: to beam is to smile broadly
deadline broken into its two parts, dead and line, each abbreviated: D for dead and L for line

explanation.surface: Someone smiles about a missed deadline in a chaotic office.
explanation.walkthrough: D (dead, as in genealogies) and L (line) are standard abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedlam was the old name of a London asylum, so it means a madhouse or uproar.

clue.text: Happy once drunk, daughter drinking wine

indicators.note: drinking means taking the wine in, so it goes inside
drunk signals the letters of once reeling into a new order

parts.note: tent is a deep red Spanish wine

explanation.surface: Someone who was cheerful when tipsy, with a daughter knocking back wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' rearranges the four letters into CONE, and with the daughter added the whole thing 'drinking' takes in the Spanish red. Tent is an old crossword favourite for wine.
explanation.definitionFit: To be contented is to be satisfied and at ease, which is a form of being happy.

clue.text: One part of a murder case's opening line

indicators.note: the opening of case is its first letter

parts.note: a row is a line, as of seats

explanation.surface: A murder investigation's first line of inquiry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'murder' is not a crime here: a murder is the collective noun for a flock of these birds.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of these black birds is called a murder, so each is one member of it.

clue.text: Return of Colonel K's hairpiece?

indicators.note: return of means the colonel abbreviation is read backwards

explanation.surface: Colonel K, Danger Mouse's boss, gets his wig back.
explanation.definitionFit: A strand of hair is a lock, and the question mark flags the playful idea of it as a piece of hair.

clue.text: Maybe 14 6 starts to crow after successful hijacking

indicators.note: starts to means the first letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: Money to gloat over after a successful hijacking.
explanation.definitionFit: A dollar note is an example of money in hand, ready to spend.

clue.text: Bugs spy sites regularly

parts.note: a mole is a spy planted inside an organisation

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of sites

explanation.surface: An agent plants listening devices at intervals around the sites.
explanation.definitionFit: To bug someone is to pester them, which is to harass or molest them.

clue.text: Ordering of a SIM card's second for female mobster?

indicators.note: ordering signals the letters being placed in a new arrangement
second means just the second letter of card

explanation.surface: A gangster's moll buying a phone SIM card.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordering' rearranges OF A SIM into MAFIOS, and the A from card follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman member of the Italian crime syndicate is given the feminine ending of the word.
